title: LEBER OPTIC ATROPHY AND DYSTONIA
alt_titles: LEBER HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY WITH DYSTONIA
DYSTONIA, FAMILIAL, WITH VISUAL FAILURE AND STRIATAL LUCENCIES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by mutation in one of several mitochondrial genes encoding subunits of complex I: MTND6 (516006), MTND4 (516003), MTND1 (516000), and MTND3 (516002).

checks.claim: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by mutation in one of several mitochondrial genes encoding subunits of complex I.
checks.evidence_quote: This family has similar clinical characteristics as the previously described families with LHON and dystonia with an ND6 mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract links LHON/dystonia to complex I genes ND1 and ND6 only. It does not support the broader claim of several genes, such as MTND4 and MTND3.

checks.claim: LDYT can be caused by mutation in MTND6.
checks.evidence_quote: The nucleotide G14459A mutation occurs in NADH dehydrogenase subunit 6, and has been suggested previously as the disease-causing mutation in Hispanic, African-American and Caucasian families of Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) and/or dystonia.
checks.explanation: The abstract names an MTND6 mutation as a cause of LHON and/or dystonia.

checks.claim: LDYT can be caused by mutation in MTND4.
checks.evidence_quote: A heteroplasmic A-->G transition at nucleotide position 11696 in the ND4 gene resulted in the substitution of an isoleucine for valine at amino acid position 312.
checks.explanation: An ND4 mutation was found and linked to the phenotype. However, it was found together with an ND6 mutation, and the paper does not show that the ND4 mutation alone is causative.

checks.claim: LDYT can be caused by mutation in MTND1.
checks.evidence_quote: The 3697G>A/ND1 mitochondrial DNA mutation causes the LHON and spastic dystonia phenotype in the same family.
checks.explanation: The paper concludes that the ND1 mutation causes LHON with spastic dystonia.

checks.claim: LDYT can be caused by mutation in MTND3.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first description of the ND3 mutation causing LDYT.

paragraphs.text: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder in which affected family members show variable combinations of vision loss, resembling Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), and progressive generalized dystonia (Wang et al., 2009). Some members of a family have both features and others have only one (Novotny et al., 1986; De Vries et al., 1996). CT scans can show bilateral symmetrical lucencies in the striatum, especially in the putamen (Marsden et al., 1986).

checks.explanation: Abstract states mitochondrial disorder but does not explicitly say maternally inherited.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-generation Hispanic family with LHON and dystonia, Jun et al. (1994) used PCR to amplify buffy coat mtDNA from a severely affected child and sequenced more than 90% of it. The mtDNA belonged to Native American haplogroup D and differed from the Cambridge sequence at 40 positions. One of these differences was a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 14459 in the ND6 gene (MTND6), which changed a moderately conserved alanine to valine at residue 72 (A72V). The variant was absent from 38 Native American haplogroup D mtDNAs and from 108 Asian, 103 Caucasian, and 99 African mtDNAs. All 6 maternal relatives tested, spanning 3 generations, carried the mutation, and 1 female relative with LHON was heteroplasmic. The authors suggested that this was the disease-causing mutation.

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) found none of the mtDNA mutations previously reported in LHON. Sequencing of the protein-coding mitochondrial genes identified 2 changes. The first was a heteroplasmic A-to-G transition at nucleotide 11696 in the ND4 gene (MTND4), which resulted in a val312-to-ile (V312I) substitution. The second was a homoplasmic T-to-A transition at nucleotide 14596 in the ND6 gene, which resulted in an ile26-to-met (I26M) substitution. A muscle biopsy from the family showed a severe complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Watanabe et al. (2006) sequenced the whole mitochondrial genome of the proband from a Japanese family with LHON and dystonia. They found 42 nucleotide changes relative to the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence. One of these was the 14459G-A mutation in the MTND6 gene, which was absent in 200 healthy Japanese controls. The authors noted that this mutation had previously been suggested to cause LHON and/or dystonia in Hispanic, African American, and Caucasian families. They stated that this was the first case of LHON with dystonia in which an mtDNA mutation had been found in a Japanese family. The proband also carried an A3203G mtDNA change, which was likewise absent in the 200 controls but was of unknown significance.

paragraphs.text: Spruijt et al. (2007) studied a family with LHON and spastic dystonia. A patient with LHON from this family did not carry any of the 3 primary LHON mutations. Screening of the patient's complete mitochondrial DNA identified a 3697G-A mutation in the ND1 gene (MTND1). The authors measured the heteroplasmy level, and the mutation seemed to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency. They concluded that the mutation caused the LHON and spastic dystonia phenotype in this family. They noted that the same mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome and suggested that other genetic factors may contribute to clinical expression.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2009) resequenced the entire mitochondrial genome by microarray in a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT. In affected members they identified a homoplasmic m.10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene, which resulted in an ala47-to-thr (A47T) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The mutation was on a haplogroup D4b background. Quantitative analysis showed that the mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side. This was the first description of an ND3 mutation causing LDYT.

paragraphs.text: Spruijt et al. (2007) screened the complete mitochondrial DNA of a patient with LHON from a family with LHON and spastic dystonia who did not carry any of the 3 primary LHON mutations. They identified a 3697G-A mutation in the MTND1 gene. The authors measured the heteroplasmy level, and the mutation seemed to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency. They concluded that the mutation caused the phenotype in this family and noted that the same mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2009) resequenced the entire mitochondrial genome by microarray in a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT. In affected members they identified a homoplasmic m.10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene, which resulted in an ala47-to-thr (A47T) substitution at a highly conserved residue, on a haplogroup D4b background. Quantitative analysis showed that the mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side. The authors noted that this mutation had also been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.
